First, § 19.2-392.2 exists in two published versions: one effective until December 1, 2026, which this memo builds against and which every expungement track records as effectiveTo 2026-11-30, and one effective December 1, 2026 which broadens the subsection A gateway to any person arrested, charged, summonsed or indicted who is not ultimately convicted provided no stipulation or judicial finding of facts sufficient to find guilt and no deferred adjudication, codifies the Commonwealth v. tracks.legalName: Petition for Expungement of Police and Court Records of a Non-Conviction, Va. Code § 19.2-392.2(A)
tracks.publicName: Expunge a Virginia charge that did not end in a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: Read at source on 2026-08-06 in the version effective until December 1, 2026, § 19.2-392.2(A) allows a person charged with a crime, a civil offence or any offence defined in Title 18.2 who is acquitted, or against whom a nolle prosequi is taken or the charge is otherwise dismissed including dismissal by accord and satisfaction under § 19.2-151, to petition for expungement of the police and court records relating to the charge, and provides that no court fees or costs are payable. Subsection C fixes venue in the circuit court of the county or city where the case was disposed of, prescribes the petition contents, and requires the petitioner to request that the CCRE electronically forward a copy of the petitioner's Virginia criminal history record to that court. Subsection D gives the attorney for the Commonwealth twenty-one days to object, answer or give written notice of no objection. Subsection F applies the manifest injustice standard but adds a presumption the controlling review could not verify: where the petitioner has no prior criminal record and the arrest was for a misdemeanor violation or the charge was a civil offence, the petitioner is entitled to expungement in the absence of good cause shown to the contrary by the Commonwealth. Subsection F also allows the court to enter the order without a hearing where the Commonwealth gives written notice of no objection and, for a felony charge, stipulates manifest injustice. Subsection K makes State Police validate the accuracy of the record but not its eligibility. Subsection L makes an order voidable within three years. Subsection M keeps the petition and any responsive pleadings under seal.

exclusions: A charge dismissed after a finding of facts sufficient for guilt, and a deferred or first-offender disposition such as a § 18.2-251 drug dismissal. Under Commonwealth v. Dotson 'otherwise dismissed' is read narrowly and this population routes to sealing instead. Exception recorded 2026-09-06 from the owner-relayed research: a dismissal under § 19.2-298.02 that all parties agreed to treat as otherwise dismissed under subsection D of that section (version in force on 2026-09-06) is evaluated under this route rather than excluded automatically; eligibility is not an order granting expungement, the agreement is never inferred, and an absent, ambiguous or disputed agreement goes to human legal review.
Convictions, other than those reached by the pardon and actual-innocence subsections, which are their own tracks.
Records where another person used the petitioner's identity, which is § 19.2-392.2(B) and a different track with a fingerprint requirement.
Juvenile records, which are a separate regime.
Federal records; Virginia relief reaches Virginia records only.

waitingPeriods.duration: None. Section 19.2-392.2 imposes no waiting period.

researchParticipantText.text: A deferred dismissal needs a closer check. A dismissal after a plea, a stipulation, or deferred proceedings does not automatically qualify. A dismissal under Virginia Code §19.2-298.02 may qualify where all parties agreed to the treatment described in subsection D. Check the court record and the agreement before selecting the dismissal ground. If the legal basis or agreement is unclear, obtain legal review before filing. Do not assume the same rule covers a dismissal under another first-offender statute.

selfHelpStopConditions: The dismissal followed a stipulation or a judicial finding of facts sufficient for guilt, or was a deferred or first-offender disposition, unless it is a dismissal under Va. Code § 19.2-298.02 that the court record shows all parties agreed to treat as otherwise dismissed under subsection D of that section (the pinned CC-1473 Rev. 07/26, Part 1, expressly includes that case in its 'otherwise dismissed' basis). legalDesignDecision.rationale: Mechanism, venue, destination, statewide scope, form identity and participant submission are settled against current primary authority, and two of the controlling review's open questions close with it. Expungement petitions are free: § 19.2-392.2(A) says so in terms, which is a stronger answer than the single clerk page the review relied on. Fingerprints do not survive for the ordinary petition: subsection C requires a CCRE electronic-forwarding request instead, and the fingerprint set is required only on a subsection (B) identity-use petition. The presumption the review could not verify is real and is in subsection F: a petitioner with no prior criminal record whose arrest was for a misdemeanor or a civil offence is entitled to expungement absent good cause shown by the Commonwealth, which materially changes what this packet can tell a participant. Two of the review's statements are corrected: the Commonwealth's window on an expungement is twenty-one days, not the thirty that applies to sealing, and the voidability period is three years, not two. The Dotson screen is implemented as a hard routing gate exactly as the review directs.

tracks.legalName: Expungement of Police and Court Records After an Absolute Pardon, Va. Code § 19.2-392.2(I)
tracks.publicName: Clear a Virginia conviction the Governor has absolutely pardoned

controllingAuthority.summary: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 19.2-392.2(I) provides that, notwithstanding any other provision of the section, upon receiving a copy pursuant to § 2.2-402 of an absolute pardon for the commission of a crime that a person did not commit, the court shall enter an order requiring expungement of the police and court records relating to the charge and conviction, and that the order shall state that the expungement is ordered pursuant to that subsection. The trigger is the court's receipt of the pardon copy, not a petition, and the outcome is mandatory. Subsection K then routes the order to State Police, who validate the accuracy of the record but expressly not its eligibility. There is no waiting period, no fee, no fingerprint step and no manifest injustice showing on this subsection.

exclusions: A conditional or partial pardon. Subsection (I) reaches an absolute pardon for the commission of a crime the person did not commit.
A simple pardon granted as an act of clemency rather than on innocence grounds, where the subsection's own words may not be satisfied.
The pardon application to the Governor itself, which is a separate executive process outside the adopted product scope.
Non-conviction charges, which are § 19.2-392.2(A) and a different track.

waitingPeriods.duration: None. Section 19.2-392.2(I) imposes no waiting period; the duty arises on the court's receipt of the pardon copy.

geography.venue: The circuit court of the county or city in which the conviction was had, which is the court that enters the § 19.2-392.2(I) order.

destination.name: Clerk of the circuit court of the locality of conviction
destination.detail: No petition is prescribed. The order issues on the court's receipt of the pardon copy transmitted under § 2.2-402. What the participant can do, and what this packet generates, is a written transmittal and request asking the court to enter the mandatory order and confirming that the pardon has been transmitted.

components.notes: Written transmittal and request to the circuit court of the locality of conviction, generated from the participant's answers, enclosing the absolute pardon, identifying the case and conviction, and asking the court to enter the order of expungement required by § 19.2-392.2(I) with the statement that the expungement is ordered pursuant to that subsection. This is not a § 19.2-392.2(A) petition and CC-1473 is not its vehicle: that form is captioned to subsection (A) alone.

Checklist naming the certified copy of the absolute pardon obtained from the Secretary of the Commonwealth, the conviction order from the circuit court file, and the participant's own CCRE record, with who issues each.

Instructions covering the § 2.2-402 transmittal route, that no fee is payable, that the outcome is mandatory once the court has the pardon, that State Police validate accuracy but not eligibility after the order, and that an order is voidable within three years for failure to strictly comply.

controllingAuthority.summary: Read at source on 2026-08-06, the exact subsection is § 19.2-392.2(B): if any person whose name or other identification has been used without his consent or authorisation by another person who has been charged or arrested using such name or identification, he may file a petition with the court disposing of the charge for relief under the section, without paying any court fees or costs, and the petition shall include one complete set of the petitioner's fingerprints obtained from a law-enforcement agency. Subsection E prescribes the proof route the controlling review could not verify: the petitioner obtains the fingerprint set from a law-enforcement agency and gives that agency a copy of the petition; the agency submits the fingerprints to the CCRE with the petition attached; the CCRE forwards the criminal history and the fingerprint set to the court under seal; on completion of the hearing the court returns the fingerprint card, and where no hearing was held the card is destroyed unless the petitioner asks for it back within thirty days or supplies a stamped self-addressed envelope. tracks.publicName: Seal an eligible minor Virginia conviction after seven clean years

controllingAuthority.summary: A free-standing petition track, not a backstop. Section 19.2-392.12:1(A) reaches an exhaustive list of offence provisions — a violation of § 4.1-305; a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-96 or § 18.2-103; a violation of § 18.2-119, § 18.2-120 or § 18.2-134; a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-248.1; a violation of subsection A of § 18.2-265.3; or a violation of § 18.2-415 — whether the disposition was a conviction or a deferred and dismissed charge, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. The single test is seven years since the date of conviction or of dismissal of the deferred charge with no conviction in that period of any law requiring a report to the CCRE under § 19.2-390(A), or of any other state, the District of Columbia, the United States or any territory, excluding Title 46.2 traffic infractions. What is not required is the whole of what makes § 19.2-392.12 hard: no manifest injustice, no rehabilitation showing, no restitution criterion, no felony-history bars, and no lifetime cap, subsection E confirming both that there is no limit on the number of petitions and that grants here do not count against the two-petition cap in § 19.2-392.12. Subsection I makes the outcome mandatory on the two findings. Subsection D carries a same-date rule: the petition may not seek sealing where the charge, conviction or ancillary matter was finalised on the same date as a conviction or deferred dismissal that is not eligible under the section. One petition may cover multiple charges, convictions and ancillary matters provided all are eligible.

exclusions: Any offence outside the exhaustive list in § 19.2-392.12:1(A).
Any offence date before 1 January 1986.
Any case where a reportable conviction occurred during the seven-year period, anywhere, other than a Title 46.2 traffic infraction.
Any charge, conviction or ancillary matter finalised on the same date as a conviction or deferred dismissal that is not eligible under the section, § 19.2-392.12:1(D).

waitingPeriods.duration: Seven years since the date of conviction or of dismissal of the deferred charge, with no reportable conviction anywhere during that period, excluding Title 46.2 traffic infractions.

The Office of the Executive Secretary publishes a CC-1201 series for sealing petitions, identified by number in the Norfolk Circuit Court Clerk's guidance of 2026-07-01. Which member of the series carries the § 19.2-392.12:1(A) petition is not pinned; see the unresolved question. The statutory content requirements are prescriptive and are what the packet fills.

The petitioner's written request that the Central Criminal Records Exchange electronically forward the petitioner's Virginia and national criminal history record to the circuit court in which the petition was filed. This replaces the fingerprint step the internal reference carried over from expungement: sealing has no fingerprint requirement. The court destroys the record after the hearing unless an appeal is noted within thirty days.

Delivery or first-class mail cover to the attorney for the Commonwealth of the filing locality, with a neutral written request that the office consider giving written notice of no objection and stipulating eligibility. The stipulation is the single most valuable thing a participant can obtain, because it lets the court enter the order without a hearing. LegalEase drafts the request; the stipulation itself is the Commonwealth's and is never generated.

controllingAuthority.summary: Petition sealing under § 19.2-392.12 reaching a conviction of, or a charge deferred and dismissed for, a misdemeanor, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. Seven years must have passed with no reportable conviction, and the clock runs from the latest of five events, not two: dismissal of the deferred charge, conviction, release from incarceration, a finding that the person violated a suspended sentence, probation or parole, or release from incarceration following such a finding. A probation violation therefore restarts the clock. Three felony-history bars apply: never convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or any other felony punishable by life; no Class 3 or 4 felony conviction within the past twenty years; and no other felony conviction within the past ten years from the date the petition was filed. Subsection C caps the section at two petitions granted in a lifetime and confines one petition to charges arising out of the same transaction or occurrence, ancillary matters not counting as separate transactions. controllingAuthority.summary: Petition sealing under § 19.2-392.12 reaching a conviction of, or a deferred and dismissed charge for, a Class 5 or 6 felony, or a violation of § 18.2-95 or any other felony offence in which the defendant is deemed guilty of larceny and punished as provided in § 18.2-95, with an offence date on or after 1 January 1986. Ten years must have passed with no reportable conviction, and the clock runs from the latest of five events, not two: dismissal of the deferred charge, conviction, release from incarceration, a finding that the person violated a suspended sentence, probation or parole, or release from incarceration following such a finding. A probation violation therefore restarts the clock. Three felony-history bars apply: never convicted of a Class 1 or 2 felony or any other felony punishable by life; no Class 3 or 4 felony conviction within the past twenty years; and no other felony conviction within the past ten years from the date the petition was filed. Four further criteria the internal reference omits entirely: rehabilitation demonstrated where the records indicate the occurrence involved the use of or dependence upon alcohol, a narcotic drug or any other self-administered intoxicant; court-ordered restitution on any charge, conviction or ancillary matter in the petition paid in full; not previously having obtained sealing of two other deferrals or convictions arising out of different sentencing events; and manifest injustice, which is a statutory condition of sealing and not merely of expungement. Subsection C caps the section at two petitions granted in a lifetime and confines one petition to charges arising out of the same transaction or occurrence, ancillary matters not counting as separate transactions. Subsection L carries a nineteen-subdivision exclusion list of enumerated Code sections. There is no fee, the Commonwealth has thirty days, a written notice of no objection stipulating eligibility and manifest injustice permits an order without a hearing, and subsection J makes an order voidable on motion within two years.

exclusions: The nineteen subdivisions of § 19.2-392.12(L), which must be encoded by Code section rather than by theme.
Subdivision L.19: any offence where the victim was a family or household member as defined in § 16.1-228.
Subdivision L.4: any non-violent felony where the person used a firearm as part of the transaction, unless firearm rights have been restored under § 18.2-308.2.
Subdivision L.16 excludes Article 3 of Chapter 8 of Title 18.2 with the exception of § 18.2-346, former subsection A of § 18.2-346, and § 18.2-347, so prostitution itself remains sealable.
Any offence date before 1 January 1986.
Any petitioner barred by the three felony-history bars.
Any petitioner who has already been granted two petitions under this section, or who has already obtained sealing of two other deferrals or convictions arising out of different sentencing events.
Any petitioner with unpaid court-ordered restitution on a matter in the petition.
Any felony other than a Class 5 or 6 felony or an § 18.2-95 larceny felony.

tracks.publicName: Some minor Virginia convictions seal themselves after seven clean years

controllingAuthority.summary: Read at source on 2026-08-06, § 19.2-392.6(A) lists the convictions ordered to be automatically sealed in the manner set out in § 19.2-392.7 where the offence date is on or after 1 January 1986: a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-96 or § 18.2-103; § 18.2-119, § 18.2-120 or § 18.2-134; a misdemeanor violation of § 18.2-248.1; or § 18.2-415. Subsection B requires seven years since the conviction date with no conviction during that period of any law requiring a CCRE report under § 19.2-390(A), or of any other state, the District of Columbia, the United States or any territory, excluding Title 46.2 traffic infractions. Subsection C blocks automatic sealing where, on the date of the conviction, the person was convicted of another offence not eligible for automatic sealing. Subsection D preserves the right to petition under § 19.2-392.12 or § 19.2-392.12:1. The section carries a second version of subsection A effective 1 July 2027 substituting 'former § 18.2-248.1', and its historical citation now includes 2026, Sp. Sess. I, c. 1.

exclusions: Any offence outside the seven provisions in § 19.2-392.6(A). In particular § 4.1-305 and subsection A of § 18.2-265.3 are on the § 19.2-392.12:1(A) petition list but NOT on the automatic list, so they can only be reached by petition.
Any offence date before 1 January 1986.
Any case where the person was convicted of an ineligible offence on the same date, § 19.2-392.6(C).
Any case where a reportable conviction occurred during the seven years.

waitingPeriods.duration: Seven years since the date of the conviction with no reportable conviction anywhere during that period, excluding Title 46.2 traffic infractions.

Marijuana possession offences and traffic infractions seal with no order at all.

components.notes: Explanation, expectation-setting and routing. Step one states what automatically seals and what does not, by Code section, and states plainly that automatic does not mean immediate. Step two states the two bars: the offence-date floor of 1 January 1986 and the same-date ineligible-conviction bar in § 19.2-392.6(C). Step three sets the operational expectation: the law is in effect from 2026-07-01 but the mechanism is phasing, State Police must build the secure verification portal by 2026-10-01, lists are compiled by electronic review and distributed at least annually, and State Police need not include an offence whose eligibility cannot be determined electronically. Step four routes: § 19.2-392.6(D) preserves the petition routes expressly, and § 19.2-392.12:1(A) covers the same offences plus two more with one arithmetic test and a mandatory outcome, so a participant who does not want to wait is offered the paid fallback honestly.

Verification plan: obtain the participant's own CCRE record, check whether the entry has in fact been sealed, and re-check on the statutory cadence rather than continuously. State Police must build the secure verification portal by 2026-10-01 and the Norfolk clerk describes automatic sealing as phasing on that date, so before then there is no participant-facing status source at all.

Fallback routing. Section 19.2-392.6(D) says expressly that automatic sealing does not prohibit a person from seeking sealing in the circuit court under § 19.2-392.12 or § 19.2-392.12:1. Where the record has not sealed, the participant is routed to the petition track that fits, and § 19.2-392.12:1(A) is tested before § 19.2-392.12 because it has no cap, no manifest injustice showing and no felony-history bars.
